Example: "Solve this equation: 2x + 3 = 7" — semantic selection query_wolfram_alpha retrieve karta hai; hierarchical me pehle Computation group select hota hai, phir uske andar query_wolfram_alpha invoke hota hai.

Tool descriptions achhi kaise likhein: concise naam (calculate_sum achha, process_numbers bura), ek-sentence summary ("Returns the sum of two numbers"), example invocation, aur input constraints (types/ranges, jaise "x and y must be integers between 0 and 1,000").

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 5
← PichhlaReAct aur Planner-ExecutorAgla →Tool Execution aur Topologies
05.4Chapter 5 — Orchestration

Tool Execution aur Topologies

Tool execution = parameters set karna (parametrization) aur tool chalana (local ya remote API). Topology = tools ko arrange karne ka pattern: Single, Parallel, Chains, ya Graphs.

  • Single tool: query → model → tool select → output → final response (4 steps). Zyada tar chatbots isi se kaam chala lete hain — simple, low latency. Pehla agent banao to wahin ruko.
  • Parallel: semantic selection se maximum 5 tools retrieve karo, model se 5 ya kam zaroori tools filter karwao, sabko independently parameterize karke parallel chalao, phir results combine karke final response. Latency bachti hai jab multiple sources se data chahiye.
  • Chains: actions ek ke baad ek, har action pichle par dependent. LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) me prompt | llm pipe syntax se chain banti hai. Chain ki maximum length set karo kyunki errors compound hote hain.
  • Graphs: nodes = tool invocation/logical step, edges = transitions (add_conditional_edges se conditional edges, consolidation edges se parallel paths merge). LangGraph me implement hota hai. Sabse expressive hain (branch + merge) lekin zyada LLM calls, latency, cost, aur cycles/unreachable paths jaise naye error classes laate hain — depth aur branching factor cap karo, pehle paper par sketch karo, har router ka unit test likho.

Parametrization kaise hoti hai: tool definition se parameters define hote hain, agent ki current state aur progress context me di jati hai, aur model se sahi data types ke saath parameters bharne ko kaha jata hai; basic parser se validate karo, galat ho to model ko correct karne ko kaho.

Examples: Weather example (Fig 5-6) — user New York City ka weather poochta hai → model weather tool select + parameterize karta hai → temperature/conditions JSON payload me aate hain → model natural-language jawab banata hai. Customer-ticket example (Fig 5-7) — parallel me customer details, order history, service logs, similar tickets aur support policies ek saath retrieve hote hain. Support graph example — categorize_issue → billing (invoice/refund) ya technical (login/performance) → summarize_response; user message "Hi, I need help with my invoice and possibly a refund", user_id "U1234", max_depth=5.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 5
← PichhlaTool Selection — Standard, Semantic, HierarchicalAgla →Context Engineering
05.5Chapter 5 — Orchestration

Context Engineering

Context engineering matlab har model invocation ke liye dynamically saare inputs — user messages, retrieved knowledge, workflow state, system prompts — ko ek structured, token-efficient context window me assemble karna, taaki har step ko sahi information mile.

4 core practices:

  • Relevance ko prioritize karo — sirf useful information retrieve karo, bade blocks indiscriminately mat chipkao.
  • Clarity — structured formatting/schemas jaise Model Context Protocol (MCP) use karo, taaki state aur retrieved knowledge predictable tareeke se mile.
  • Summarization — lambi history ko compress karo, critical details bachakar.
  • Dynamic assembly — har inference step par context ko current objective, workflow stage aur user input ke hisaab se dobara banao.

Kyun matter karta hai: book kehta hai — jaise-jaise foundation models improve ho rahe hain, agentic design ka frontier model architecture se hatkar context ki quality par shift ho raha hai. Achha context modest model ki bhi poori capacity unlock kar deta hai; kharab context sabse advanced model ko bhi undermine kar sakta hai. Context engineering memory, knowledge aur orchestration ke beech ka glue hai.

Prompt engineering se farak: prompt engineering instructions likhna hai; context engineering poora context dynamically assemble karna hai — kya, kitna, aur kis order me model ko dena hai.

Example: ecommerce support agent ka context = system prompt (allowed actions) + user ka current message + order record ka retrieved summary + applicable policy excerpts; advanced systems me prior related conversations ke summaries aur pehle ke tool calls ke results bhi judte hain.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 5
← PichhlaTool Execution aur TopologiesAgla →Chapter 6 — Knowledge and Memory
06Part 2 — Create, Orchestrate, Scale

Chapter 6 — Knowledge and Memory

Memory agentic systems ke successful operation ke liye critical hai. Recent interactions context window bahut se use cases ke liye kaafi hai, lekin challenging scenarios me robust approach — semantic memory, GraphRAG, working memory — me investment fayda deta hai.

Is chapter me: context windows aur rolling window (sabse simple memory), full-text search (BM25) vs semantic search, RAG (indexing + runtime), semantic experience memory, GraphRAG aur knowledge graphs, aur note-taking (self-notes) — ek cheap trick jo reasoning improve karta hai.

Book ka ek important point: memory sirf data store karna nahi hai — woh badalta hai ki agent environment aur end users se kaise interact karta hai. Aur ek debated sawal: bade models, bade context windows aur zyada compute elaborate text search aur vector DBs ko obsolete kar sakte hain — lekin abhi ke liye hybrid hi best practice hai, khaas taur par jab memory freshness ya precision ranking critical ho.

Chapter ka core idea

Agent ko yaad rakhna chahiye — lekin kya yaad rakhe, kaise retrieve kare, aur kab bhool jaye, yahi memory design hai. Context window se shuru karo, zaroorat pade to RAG, phir GraphRAG.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 6
← PichhlaContext EngineeringAgla →Context Windows aur Rolling Window
06.1Chapter 6 — Knowledge and Memory

Context Windows aur Rolling Window

Context window = ek call me foundation model ko di gayi saari information; context length = maximum tokens jo model ek call me ingest/attend kar sakta hai. Ye us request ki working memory hai.

Rolling context window me interaction aage badhne par sabse purana context FIFO tareeke se eject hokar newest se replace hota hai. Simplest approach me context window me current question + current session ki saari previous interactions hoti hain; window bhar jaye to sirf most recent interactions rehti hain. Token budget allocate karna padta hai jab information window se zyada ho.

Numbers yaad rakhna: 1 token ≈ ¾ word ya ~4 characters; 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 English words. Limits: 4,000 tokens ≈ 3,000 words (~12 pages); 8,000 tokens ≈ 6,000 words (~24 pages); GPT-5 aur Claude 3.7 Sonnet 272,000 tokens input; Gemini 2.5 up to 1 million tokens input.

Drawback: relevant/important information bhi eject ho jati hai jab kaafi interaction ho jaye; lambi prompts me model important information miss bhi kar sakta hai — isliye most relevant context ko prompt ke end ke paas rakhna help karta hai.

Example (book ka demo): LangGraph example me user kehta hai "hi! I'm [Name]" aur phir poochta hai "what's my name?" — bina persistent state ke model naam bhool jata hai. Isiliye sirf context window kaafi nahi hoti; state ko explicitly maintain karna padta hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 6
← PichhlaChapter 6 — Knowledge and MemoryAgla →Full-Text Search (BM25) vs Semantic Search
06.2Chapter 6 — Knowledge and Memory

Full-Text Search (BM25) vs Semantic Search

Traditional full-text search inverted index par chalta hai — tokenization, normalization (lowercasing, stemming), stop-word removal; har term → us term wale chunks ki list — aur BM25 se rank karta hai. BM25 har passage ko weight deta hai: term frequency (query term kitni baar aaya), inverse document frequency (term corpus me kitna rare hai), aur document length normalization (bahut lambe/chhote chunks ko penalize).

Semantic search meaning samajhta hai — embeddings se, exact keywords mile bina bhi relevant results laata hai. Text ko dense vector (embedding) me convert karte hain — Word2Vec, GloVe, BERT jaise models, aur LLMs ne embedding quality aur badha di; semantically similar words high-dimensional space me paas hote hain.

Kab kaunsa: keyword search exact/specific terms pinpoint karne me excellent hai, lekin paraphrases, broader themes ya conceptual links miss kar deta hai jo original text me usi shabd me nahi likhe gaye. Semantic memory agent ko related ideas recall karne deti hai chahe exact words alag hon.

Example (BM25): 3 lines ka corpus — ek fresh recruit agent, ek experienced agent, aur galaxy ko bachane wale 2 agents; query "Who is a recruit?" top 2 lines deti hai.

Example (semantic): "Machine learning is a method of data analysis…" aur "Artificial intelligence (AI) is the simulation of human intelligence…" save karke query "What is the relationship between AI and machine learning?" — top_n=3 results milte hain, bina exact keywords ke.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 6
← PichhlaContext Windows aur Rolling WindowAgla →RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation
06.3Chapter 6 — Knowledge and Memory

RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation

RAG retrieval-based methods aur generative models ko combine karta hai: pehle relevant information retrieve karo, phir use context ke saath generative foundation model ko do taaki woh informed, accurate jawab banaye.

Indexing pipeline (Fig 6-1): source documents → smaller chunks me todo → har chunk ko encoder model se dense embedding banao → vectors ko vector database me store karo.

Runtime (Fig 6-2): user question controller ko jati hai → vector knowledge store se most relevant information retrieve hoti hai → retrieved context + original question generative model ko milta hai → final contextually informed response.

Kyun matter karta hai: RAG agent ko model weights ke bahar ki verifiable, domain- ya company-specific information (technical specs, policy documents, product catalogs, logs) use karne deta hai; hallucination kam hoti hai aur jawab grounded rehta hai. Ye domain/company-specific information ya policies ko output par influence karne ke liye khaas taur par valuable hai.

Chunking ka idea: model ko poori lambi resource nahi chahiye — sirf chhota relevant hissa chahiye, jaise insaan ko. Vector stores: VectorDB, FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search), Annoy (Approximate Nearest Neighbors Oh Yeah).

Semantic experience memory: past interactions ko embed karke store karo; har naye input par best matches ko context window ka hissa banao — context window ka ek hissa best matches ke liye reserve rehta hai, baaki system message, latest user input aur most recent interactions ke liye.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 6
← PichhlaFull-Text Search (BM25) vs Semantic SearchAgla →GraphRAG aur Knowledge Graphs
06.4Chapter 6 — Knowledge and Memory

GraphRAG aur Knowledge Graphs

GraphRAG RAG ka advanced extension hai jo graph-based data structures use karta hai: dataset se entities aur relationships ka knowledge graph banata hai, phir multihop reasoning, relationship chaining aur structured summarization karta hai. Knowledge graph me entities nodes hote hain aur relationships edges.

Knowledge graph banane ke 8 steps: (1) data collection, (2) data preprocessing, (3) entity recognition/extraction (NER — named entity recognition), (4) relationship extraction, (5) ontology design (schema: entity types aur possible relationship types), (6) graph population (Neo4j, OrientDB, Amazon Neptune), (7) integration and validation (entity resolution — duplicate entities link karna), (8) maintenance and updates. Triples Resource Description Framework (RDF) data model ke subject-predicate-object form me extract hote hain; foundation models triples extract karne me kaafi achhe hain, isliye graphs ab scale par ban sakte hain.

Baseline RAG kab fail hota hai: jab answer multiple documents me bikhri information ko connect karke banta ho ("connecting the dots"), query poore dataset ke higher-level themes ka summary maange, ya dataset bada/messy/narrative ho. GraphRAG inme behtar hai — lekin zyada expensive aur complex hai; book kehta hai standard chunking + vector retrieval jab limit me aaye, tab GraphRAG try karo. Prototype banana easy hai, production-ready karna significant undertaking hai.

Example: "[Name] ne kya kiya hai?" — baseline RAG fail ho sakta hai kyunki koi ek chunk uske actions ko comprehensively cover nahi karta; GraphRAG graph se jawab bana sakta hai. Microsoft GraphRAG CLI: pip install graphrag, graphrag init --root ./ragtest, graphrag index, phir graphrag query --method global ya --method local.

Neo4j Cypher example: Concepts (Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Neural Networks, Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing), Tools (TensorFlow, PyTorch), Models (BERT year 2018, ResNet year 2015); relationships SUBSET_OF, USED_IN, APPLICATION_OF, IMPLEMENTS, BELONGS_TO, BUILT_WITH; shortestPath query NLP se Deep Learning tak. Neo4j ke strengths: native graph storage, index-free adjacency, near-constant traversal performance billions of nodes/relationships par bhi, ACID compliance.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 6
← PichhlaRAG — Retrieval-Augmented GenerationAgla →Dynamic Knowledge Graphs, Long Context, Note-Taking
06.5Chapter 6 — Knowledge and Memory

Dynamic Knowledge Graphs, Long Context, Note-Taking

Dynamic knowledge graphs continuously new information se update hote rehte hain (real-time data integrate karte hain). Fayde: real-time information processing (news, social media, live monitoring), adaptive learning bina retraining ke (medicine, technology, finance jaise fast-evolving fields). Risks: maintenance complexity (errors/inconsistencies propagate ho sakti hain), resource intensity, security/privacy concerns (real-time data se compliance mushkil), dependency/overreliance (graph me jo nahi hai, woh miss ho sakta hai). Mitigations: robust validation/automated checks, scalable architecture (distributed DBs, cloud), encryption/access controls/anonymization, critical decisions me human oversight.

Long-context models (retrieval-free): poori knowledge base seedha prompt me load kar lete hain — Gemini 2.5 aur GPT-4.1 up to 1M tokens (~750,000 words, 2,500+ pages) support karte hain. Lekin itne tokens process karna compute/latency/cost me mehenga hai, aur guarantee nahi ki model ek relevant piece dhoondh hi lega. Community consensus: hybrid architectures ki value bani hui hai (extended context + selective retrieval).

Note-taking (self-notes): model ko pehle context par notes likhne ko kaha jata hai, phir question ka jawab banata hai — standard approach (context + question → answer) aur chain-of-thought se alag; experiments me multiple reasoning/evaluation tasks par good results. Cheap trick hai jo reasoning improve karta hai bina kisi infrastructure ke.

Fig 6-5 me standard vs self-note workflow compare hota hai — note-taking wale flow me model pehle notes banata hai, phir un notes + question se final answer deta hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 6
← PichhlaGraphRAG aur Knowledge GraphsAgla →Chapter 7 — Learning in Agentic Systems
07Part 2 — Create, Orchestrate, Scale

Chapter 7 — Learning in Agentic Systems

Agent experience se kaise seekhta hai? Learning ke do tareeke hain: nonparametric — model parameters badle bina experience se seekhna (examples, reflections, insights ko prompt/memory me daal kar) — aur parametric — model weights ko directly fine-tune karke deeper specialization.

Is chapter me: exemplar learning (fixed vs dynamic few-shot), Reflexion (agent apna khud ka coach), experiential learning / ExpeL (insights nikaalo, promote/demote karo), aur fine-tuning — SFT, DPO, RLVR, aur chhote models ka promise.

Book ki pehli salah: learning capability add karna useful hai lekin necessary nahi — extra design, evaluation aur monitoring chahiye, jo application ke hisaab se worth ho bhi sakti hai aur nahi bhi. Aur ek famous line: "When in doubt, don't fine-tune your model." Pehle dekho kya existing pretrained/instruction-tuned model prompt engineering ya nonparametric learning se kaam kar leta hai.

Chapter ka core idea

Nonparametric = sasta, fast, transparent — pehle yahi try karo. Parametric = deep specialization — tab jab data, budget aur use case demand kare. Dono ko combine karke intelligent, robust agents banao.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 7
← PichhlaDynamic Knowledge Graphs, Long Context, Note-TakingAgla →Nonparametric vs Parametric Learning
07.1Chapter 7 — Learning in Agentic Systems

Nonparametric vs Parametric Learning

Nonparametric learning = performance improve karo bina model ke parameters badle — examples, reflections, insights ko prompt/memory me daal kar. Parametric learning = foundation model ke parameters ko train/fine-tune karke improve karo.

Nonparametric kaise kaam karta hai: successful examples ko few-shot examples ki tarah prompt me do; reflections/insights ko memory buffer me rakho; retrieval se relevant examples lao. Simple, fast, cheap hai — pehle yahi try karo.

Parametric kaise kaam karta hai: SFT (prompt, ideal-response pairs), DPO (good vs bad response pairs), RFT/RLVR (grader ke scores par policy update). Tab karo jab examples kaafi hon (hundreds to thousands curated examples) aur prompt engineering kaam na kare; usme GPU hours, expert graders, version management aur retraining schedules ka kharcha hai.

Table 7-1 (book): fine-tuning ke primary methods — SFT (supervised fine-tuning), Vision fine-tuning, DPO (direct preference optimization), RFT (reinforcement fine-tuning) / RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) — har ek ka how-it-works aur best-for alag hai.

Kab karein, kab na karein: Fine-tune karo jab domain specialization critical ho (organization jargon, strict style guide), consistent tone/format chahiye (financial disclosures, legal disclaimers), tool/API calls precise hone chahiye (medical dosages, trading APIs), sufficient high-quality data + budget ho, aur retraining frequency manageable ho. Hold off karo jab rapid prototyping/low-volume ho, model evolution effort ko invalidate kar sakti ho (naya model update fine-tuned purane model se behtar ho sakta hai), ya resource constraints hon.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 7
← PichhlaChapter 7 — Learning in Agentic SystemsAgla →Exemplar Learning — Fixed vs Dynamic Few-Shot
07.2Chapter 7 — Learning in Agentic Systems

Exemplar Learning — Fixed vs Dynamic Few-Shot

Exemplar learning me agent apne kaam ke dauraan quality measure ke saath examples collect karta hai; successful examples ko future prompts me few-shot examples ki tarah use karta hai.

Fixed few-shot me examples prompt me hardcoded rehte hain aur badalte nahi. Dynamic few-shot me runtime par vector database se most relevant examples retrieve hote hain (Fig 7-1). Har stored case = problem description + applied solution + outcome. Naye situation par agent memory me similar past cases dhoondhta hai, unke solutions ko analyze karta hai aur zaroorat par adapt karta hai.

Kyun matter karta hai: simple, transparent, lightweight — bina retraining ke rapid improvement. Successful examples persistent storage me save karo, phir retrieve karke prompt me do — performance significantly badhti hai, ye well-established finding hai, multiple domains me confirm hui hai. Ye poore agentic task par ya task ke subsets par independently apply ho sakta hai.

Trade-off: examples badhne par cost aur latency badhti hai, aur har example har input ke liye useful nahi hota — isliye dynamic selection. Examples badhne par type/text/semantic retrieval se most relevant examples chuno.

Example: memory bank me har interaction ka context, actions, outcomes aur feedback store hota hai — jaise human memory, jahan past experiences future decisions guide karti hain.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 7
← PichhlaNonparametric vs Parametric LearningAgla →Reflexion — Agent Apna Khud Ka Coach
07.3Chapter 7 — Learning in Agentic Systems

Reflexion — Agent Apna Khud Ka Coach

Reflexion me agent har unsuccessful attempt ke baad ek chhota sa written reflection likhta hai — kya galat hua, agli baar kya alag karna hai — aur use "memory buffer" me rakhta hai. Agli attempt se pehle recent reflections dobara padhta hai, bina model retrain kiye strategy adjust karta hai.

5 steps: (1) action sequence perform karo; (2) trial log karo — actions, observations, success/failure persistent storage (JSON file ya DB table) me; (3) reflection generate karo — failed trial par reflection prompt banao ("What strategy did I miss? What should I do differently next time?"); (4) memory update karo — update_memory helper logs padhkar LLM se reflection banwakar memory me save karta hai (last 3 reflections tak bounded); (5) next run par reflections ko prompt me prepend karo. Numerical feedback (success flag) aur free-form comments dono chalte hain.

Kyun matter karta hai: bahut lightweight — model weights ko chhede bina, foundation model ko apna coach bana do. Code debugging se lekar multistep reasoning tak performance boost dikha hai. Book kehta hai poora approach "just a few lines of code" / "under 20 lines" me implement ho jata hai.

Example (book): dairy-free aur apple variety pack of chips, price $30 se kam — agent search karta hai, galat item (Lentil Chips Variety Pack, $100.0) par click karta hai, "Buy Now" click karta hai, STATUS: FAIL. Reflection prompt me poora Action/Observation transcript + "Plan:" cue hota hai, jisse model concise corrective plan likhta hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 7
← PichhlaExemplar Learning — Fixed vs Dynamic Few-ShotAgla →Experiential Learning / ExpeL
07.4Chapter 7 — Learning in Agentic Systems

Experiential Learning / ExpeL

Experiential learning Reflexion se ek kadam aage hai: experiences collect karke unse insights aggregate karta hai jo future policy improve karte hain — cross-task learning. ExpeL insights ki list maintain karta hai; naye insights add hote hain, existing edit/upvote/downvote/remove hote hain.

Kaise kaam karta hai: model se observation par reflect karwakar insight generate karo (InsightAgent.generate_insight). Phir rules ko reevaluate karo — AGREE <NUMBER>: <RULE>, REMOVE <NUMBER>: <RULE>, EDIT <NUMBER>: <NEW RULE>, ADD <NEW NUMBER>: <NEW RULE>. Insights ko successful vs unsuccessful trial pairs se extract karke distill kiya jata hai — chhoti si list of general, high-level critiques/rules (Fig 7-4).

Kyun matter karta hai: agent tasks ke beech transfer kar sakta hai — ek task me seekhi good practice doosre task me kaam aati hai. Nonstationary (badalte hue) environments me gradual adaptation possible hai. Practical, affordable, easy to implement, continual adaptation deta hai.

Example (book): simulated reports — website traffic +15% lekin bounce rate 40% → 55% (target miss — demote); email open rates 25% (20% goal se upar — promote); cart abandonment 60% → 68% (50% target miss — demote); average order value +8% (5% uplift target se upar — promote); new subscriptions −5% (10% growth goal se neeche — demote). Promoted insight ko human-in-the-loop edit karke refine kiya jata hai ("Investigate landing-page UX changes to reduce bounce").

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 7
← PichhlaReflexion — Agent Apna Khud Ka CoachAgla →Fine-Tuning — SFT, DPO, RLVR, Chhote Models
07.5Chapter 7 — Learning in Agentic Systems

Fine-Tuning — SFT, DPO, RLVR, Chhote Models

Fine-tuning = pretrained model ko task-specific dataset par adapt karna, parameters me chhote adjustments karke. SFT (prompt, ideal-response) pairs se sikhati hai; DPO (good vs bad) preference pairs se model ko better outputs prefer karna sikhata hai; RFT/RLVR expert graders ke verifiable rewards par policy-gradient-style updates se complex reasoning reinforce karta hai.

SFT example: function calling fine-tune karo — model seekhta hai kab call karna hai aur kab nahi (jaise "What's the weather in Boston?" → get_weather(location="Boston") call karo; lekin "Imagine it's snowing in Boston—what should I wear?" par hypothetical jawab do, real call mat karo). Schema discipline: JSON Schema / TypeScript/Zod se har function ka contract define karo; runtime par Zod, Ajv ya Pydantic se har proposed call validate karo. Special tokens: reasoning ko <think>…</think> me, calls ko <tool_call>…</tool_call> me wrap karo. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters + SFTTrainer (Hugging Face TRL) se efficient training.

DPO example: microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct base model, IT help-desk dataset ({prompt, chosen, rejected} rows), LoRA r=8, lora_alpha=16, dropout 0.05, lr 5e-6, 3 epochs, beta 0.1, loss sigmoid, max_length 8192. Prompt → multiple completions → humans rank karte hain (y_win / y_lose preference data) → DPO training directly preferred outputs ki taraf optimize karta hai.

RLVR: prompts se multiple completions → grader (automated ya human) rewards deta hai → trainer policy update karta hai; DPO se aage — value scores predict karke observed rankings se beyond generalize karta hai. Book me RLVR ka full code nahi hai — repo me hai.

Chhote models ka promise: fewer parameters, faster adaptation, zyada interpretable (finance/healthcare/regulatory me explainability), Agile iterations, edge/mobile/IoT aur federated learning par deployment, kam energy (green AI), aur narrow tasks par fine-tuned hokar bade models jaisi performance de sakte hain. Benchmarks (early 2025, Stanford HELM): DeepSeek-v3 aur Llama 3.1 Instruct Turbo (70B) MMLU mean >66%; Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite (8B) ~64% threshold; Phi-3-mini (3.8B) ne 540B-parameter PaLM ke 60% MMLU score ko match kiya — 142× size reduction in two years.

Pretraining (trillions of tokens par scratch se training) sirf major AI labs ka kaam hai — almost sab teams ko high-quality open source models se start karna chahiye.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 7
← PichhlaExperiential Learning / ExpeLAgla →Chapter 8 — From One Agent to Many
08Part 2 — Create, Orchestrate, Scale

Chapter 8 — From One Agent to Many

Single-agent se multiagent transition complex tasks, adaptability aur efficiency me fayda deta hai — lekin har agent ke saath scalability challenges aate hain jinke liye careful planning chahiye.

Is chapter me: single-agent vs multiagent (kab ek kaafi hai), 6 principles for adding agents, coordination strategies (democratic, manager, hierarchical, actor-critic), ADAS (agents khud agents design karen), aur communication — A2A protocol, message brokers, actor frameworks, workflow engines, aur state/persistence.

Book ki pehli salah: simple se start karo, complexity sirf tab add karo jab performance improve karni ho. Pehle single-agent ke andar scale karne ki koshish karo — hierarchical tool selection ya semantic tool selection (Ch 5); woh bhi fail ho to agents me decompose karo.

Chapter ka core idea

Communication implementation detail nahi hai — first-class concern hai jo decide karta hai agents kaise perceive/respond/collaborate karte hain. Simple settings me in-memory queues kaafi hain; production me message brokers, actor frameworks aur workflow engines state, retries aur execution durability manage karte hain.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 8
← PichhlaFine-Tuning — SFT, DPO, RLVR, Chhote ModelsAgla →Single-Agent vs Multiagent
08.1Chapter 8 — From One Agent to Many

Single-Agent vs Multiagent

Single-agent system me ek agent saare tools aur decisions sambhalta hai; multiagent me multiple agents shared goals ke liye collaborate karte hain, aur har ek ka apna specialized role hota hai.

Single-agent kab best hai: jab difficulty modest ho, tools limited hon, environment lower-complexity wala ho, ya latency critical ho — tab single-agent best hai. Ek agent tools invoke karta hai, limit tak, phir user ko jawab deta hai. Simple hai, sasta hai, kam latency hai — isliye core functionality jaldi validate hoti hai.

Multiagent kab fayda deta hai: jab tasks complex hon, varied toolsets chahiye hon, parallel processing ya dynamic environments hon — tab multiagent fayda deta hai. Specialization se har agent apne strength par focus karta hai; tools aur responsibilities distribute karne se single-agent ki limits solve hoti hain — jaise bada toolset hone par galat tool selection hota hai.

Example (book — supply chain): single agent ke paas 16 tools hain (manage_inventory, track_shipments, evaluate_suppliers, optimize_warehouse, forecast_demand, manage_quality, arrange_shipping, coordinate_operations, manage_special_handling, handle_compliance, process_returns, scale_operations, optimize_costs, optimize_delivery, manage_disruption, send_logistics_response). Example query: "We're running critically low on SKU-12345. Current stock is 50 units but we have 200 units on backorder. What's our reorder strategy?" — operation_id "OP-12345", type inventory_management, priority high, location "Warehouse A". 16 tools hone par system prompt me saari possibilities describe karni padti hain — isliye confusion aur suboptimal choices badhte hain.

Multiagent version: 16 tools 3 specialists me bante hain — Inventory & Warehouse (7 tools), Transportation & Logistics (8 tools), Supplier & Compliance (3 tools, shared send_logistics_response ke saath) — matlab har specialist ke paas sirf apne kaam ke tools hote hain, isliye confusion kam hota hai aur sahi tool choose karna aasan hota hai.

Swarms: nature se inspired hain (flocks of birds, schools of fish, colonies of ants) — large numbers of simple agents, minimal individual intelligence, emergent behavior via local interactions; advantages hain scalability (hundreds ya thousands agents), robustness (no single point of failure), flexibility, aur distributed problem-solving. Matlab chhote chhote agents milke bada kaam karte hain.

Yaad rakho: single-agent tab best hai jab kaam chhota ho aur tools kam hon — matlab jaldi validate karna ho to ek agent kaafi hai. Lekin jab kaam bada ho, tools zyada hon, ya kaam parallel me karna ho, tab multiagent best hai — kyunki har agent apna kaam karta hai aur sab milke bada kaam poora karte hain.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 8
← PichhlaChapter 8 — From One Agent to ManyAgla →Principles for Adding Agents — 6 Siddhant
08.2Chapter 8 — From One Agent to Many

Principles for Adding Agents — 6 Siddhant

Agents add karte waqt book ke 6 principles:

  • Task decomposition — complex task ko chhote manageable subtasks me todo, clear boundaries se overlap/redundancy kam.
  • Specialization — har agent ko uski strength wala role do.
  • Parsimony — sirf minimal number of agents add karo jo functionality/performance ke liye zaroori hon; har agent communication overhead, coordination complexity aur resource demands badhata hai; pehle socho kya kaam existing agents se ho sakta hai. Parsimony khaas taur par interview me poochha jane wala principle hai.
  • Coordination — robust communication protocols + conflict resolution protocols.
  • Robustness — redundancy: fail hone par doosra agent takeover kare; network failures/agent downtime jhel sake.
  • Efficiency — har agent addition ke cost-benefit ko weigh karo.

Kyun matter karta hai: bina principles ke agent proliferation hoti hai — maintenance burden aur performance bottlenecks badhte hain. Lean system hi sustainable hota hai.

Example: supply chain disruption during peak season — supervisor query ko transportation specialist ko route karta hai (immediate containment), jabki inventory specialist concurrently warehouse operations scale karta hai — dynamic rerouting aur parallelism ka example; ek agent fail ho (API downtime) to poora process rukta nahi.

Book kehta hai software architecture ke wahi lessons yahan bhi apply hote hain jo monolith ko todne me seekhe the — agents ko independently validate, test, integrate aur reuse kiya ja sake.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 8
← PichhlaSingle-Agent vs MultiagentAgla →Coordination Strategies
08.3Chapter 8 — From One Agent to Many

Coordination Strategies

Democratic: saare agents equal decision-making power rakhte hain, consensus se decide karte hain, koi leader nahi. Decentralized, no single point of failure, flexible, fair — lekin consensus me extensive communication, slow decisions, complex protocol. Best fit: distributed sensor networks, collaborative robotics (fairness/robustness).

Manager: ek (ya zyada) manager agents subordinates ko oversee karte hain, tasks distribute karte hain, conflicts resolve karte hain. Streamlined decisions, clear task assignment, simple communication (subordinates sirf manager se baat karte hain) — lekin single point of failure, manager bottleneck ban sakta hai, adaptability kam. Best fit: manufacturing, customer support centers (structured, centralized control).

Hierarchical: multiple levels — upar wale strategic decisions, neeche wale tactical execution, subordinates ko kuch autonomy. Scalability (coordination distribute hoti hai), redundancy, clear authority — lekin design complex, multiple levels se communication delays aur latency. Best fit: supply chain management, military operations (large, complex systems).

Actor-Critic: actor candidate outputs banata hai, critic rubric/checklist se accept/reject karta hai, threshold mile tab tak iterate karta hai. Test-time compute ka form — actor 3 candidate plans banata hai (JSON list), critic feasibility/cost/risk par 1–10 score karta hai, best score > 8 ho to execute karo, warna "Regenerate with improvements: <feedback>" loop. Best fit: jab evaluation generation se aasan ho ("yeh achha output hai" kehna aasan, pehli baar me banana mushkil).

Example: supply chain supervisor node — prompt me team members list (inventory / transportation / supplier) aur instruction "select ONE team member… Output ONLY the selected member's name"; route_to_specialist function supervisor ke output ko padhkar conditional edge se specialist ko route karta hai, warna END.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 8
← PichhlaPrinciples for Adding Agents — 6 SiddhantAgla →ADAS — Automated Design of Agent Systems
08.4Chapter 8 — From One Agent to Many

ADAS — Automated Design of Agent Systems

ADAS handcrafted architectures se hatkar aisi systems ki taraf shift hai jo khud ko design, evaluate aur iteratively improve kar sakti hain. Meta Agent Search (MAS) algorithm ek higher-level meta-agent se automatically agentic systems create, assess aur refine karwata hai.

3 core components (Fig 8-1): search space (representable agentic architectures ka scope), search algorithm (exploration strategy), evaluation function (performance/robustness/efficiency ke against candidate agents ko quantify karna). Agents ko code se define kiya jata hai — Turing-complete languages se theoretically koi bhi structure/behavior invent ho sakta hai.

MAS cycle: meta-agent archive of prior agents ko dekhkar high-level design description generate karta hai → code me implement karta hai ("forward" function) → novelty aur correctness ke liye 2 self-reflection steps → validation data par evaluate karta hai → errors par up to 5 debugging refinements → successful agents archive hote hain performance metrics (accuracy ya F1) ke saath. Loop 25–30 generations chal sakta hai. Evaluation: generated code ko exec se load karke forward function banaya jata hai, task data par parallel (ThreadPoolExecutor) evaluate kiya jata hai, fitness = bootstrap confidence interval of accuracy list.

Results (book): ARC (grid-transformation puzzles) par MAS ne CoT, Self-Refine, LLM-Debate ko beat kiya. Reasoning benchmarks: DROP (reading comprehension) F1 79.4 ± 0.8 (+13.6 over Role Assignment baseline); MGSM (math) 53.4% ± 3.5 accuracy (+14.4% over LLM-Debate); MMLU 69.6% ± 3.2 (+2% over OPRO prompt optimization); GPQA (science) 34.6% ± 3.2 (+1.7% over OPRO). MAS-discovered agents hand-designed baselines se behtar perform karte hain aur cross-domain transfer karte hain (ARC par discover kiye agents MMLU par bhi chalte hain; GPT-3.5 se GPT-4 par switch karne par bhi performance bani rehti hai) — isse lagta hai ye agents narrow tricks nahi, general principles embody karte hain.

Concerns: safety, reliability, alignment with human values; autonomy aur constraint ka balance zaroori hai. Paper: "Automated Design of Agentic Systems", International Conference on Learning Representations, Singapore, April 2025. (Paper ke author names SPA me nahi dikhaye gaye hain.)

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 8
← PichhlaCoordination StrategiesAgla →Communication — A2A, Brokers, Actors, Workflows
08.5Chapter 8 — From One Agent to Many

Communication — A2A, Brokers, Actors, Workflows

Jaise system single-device prototype se distributed production me jata hai, communication architecture critical ho jata hai — matlab ab ye decide karna zaroori hai ki agents aapas me kaise baat karenge. Options hain: local (in-memory/function calls/shared memory), A2A Protocol (standardized agent discovery/negotiation), message brokers/event buses (async decoupling), actor frameworks (state + messaging unified), workflow engines (durable orchestration), aur state/persistence choices — matlab pehle hi sochna padta hai ki agents aapas me kaise baat karenge, warna baad me poora design badalna padta hai.

A2A (Google): har agent ek machine-readable JSON Agent Card publish karta hai (identity, capabilities jaise generateReport/summarizeLegalDocument, input/output schemas, endpoint, auth methods jaise OAuth 2/API key, version, optional metadata) — well-known endpoint /.well-known/agent.json par serve hoti hai; registry se discover karo, handshake karo (version/capability check), phir JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTPS se structured requests bhejo (transport-agnostic — gRPC/WebSocket bhi possible). Abhi ye infancy me hai: authorization, rate-limiting, trust establishment, abuse resistance — ye sab far from solved hain, matlab abhi in par bahut kaam baaki hai. Example: SummarizerAgent, capability summarizeText, endpoint http://localhost:8000/api, version 1.0; JSON-RPC id 123, method summarizeText, max_tokens 150, temperature 0.7, model gpt-4o; error code −32601 "Method not found". Matlab A2A se agents ek doosre ko dhoondh sakte hain aur baat kar sakte hain — lekin abhi ye naya hai, isliye production me use karne se pehle iski limits samajhna zaroori hai.

Message brokers: Kafka (high-throughput distributed event streaming, durability, topic partitioning, consumer groups, replayable log); Redis Stream aur RabbitMQ (lightweight, lower throughput, tighter latency, easier deployment; Redis memory-based hai, isliye durability limited hai); NATS (lightweight cloud-native, low-latency high-throughput, pub/sub + request/reply, JetStream se durable streams/replay). Redis example: supervisor supply-chain-tasks stream me task publish karta hai (xadd), specialists xread se consume karte hain, supply-chain-responses me jawab dete hain; wait_for_response timeout 60s. Matlab broker beech me khada hokar agents ko alag rakhta hai — ek agent fail bhi ho to doosra apna kaam karta rehta hai, aur messages kho nahi jaate.

Actor frameworks: Ray (Python-native, @ray.remote, async method invocations, resource-aware scheduling, fault tolerance via restarts/retries), Orleans (virtual actor model, .NET, automatic instantiation/suspension/recovery, state persistence minimal boilerplate), Akka (JVM Java/Scala, classic actor model, Akka Cluster — sharding, persistence, supervision, adaptive load balancing; telecom/trading production use). Actor tab worth hain jab agents 10–20 se zyada hon ya latency demands tight hon — matlab tab inko use karna sahi rehta hai, kyunki har agent ka apna state hota hai aur woh messages se baat karta hai.

Workflow engines: Temporal (durable stateful workflows, retries, failure recovery, activities, RetryPolicy maximum_attempts=3, 30s start_to_close_timeout; crash ke baad last successful step se resume hota hai), Apache Airflow (DAGs, batch/time-triggered, ETL/ML training — real-time/dynamic agent interactions ke liye nahi hai), Dagger (workflows as code with containers, caching, type safety, local→CI/CD→production consistency). Matlab workflow engine ka kaam hai ki lamba kaam beech me ruk bhi jaaye to wahi se phir se shuru ho — isliye durable workflows ke liye ye best hai.

State/persistence (Table 8-1): relational DBs (PostgreSQL/Redis — flexible, queryable, cost-effective; manual management, potential inconsistency); vector stores (Pinecone — semantic search, scalable embeddings; higher cost, specialized setup); object storage (S3/Azure Blob — cheap, durable, large data; slow access, no native indexing); stateful orchestration frameworks (Temporal/Orleans — automated recovery, low boilerplate; framework lock-in). Memory types hain: episodic (short-lived, task-specific — in-memory/transient kaafi hai), semantic (long-term knowledge — durable storage + vector indexing chahiye), workflow durability (mid-process failure resilience — Temporal/Orleans checkpointing). Matlab sahi storage tab chuno jab tumhe pata ho ki data kitna bada hai, kitni der rakhna hai, aur kitni jaldi chahiye — galat choice baad me bahut mehenga padta hai.

Kyun matter karta hai: point-to-point communication scale par brittle ho jata hai; broker se loose coupling, independent scaling, fault tolerance (replay missed messages) aur naye agents add karna aasan hota hai — lekin eventual consistency aur complex error handling ki keemat par, matlab ye fayde free me nahi milte — broker hi woh cheez hai jo bade system ko sambhalta hai, bina broker ke har agent ko har doosre agent se seedha baat karni padti hai.

Yaad rakho: chhote system me simple calls kaafi hain, lekin jaise jaise agents badhte hain, communication ka design utna hi zaroori hota hai — pehle hi sahi tareeka chuno, baad me badalna mushkil hota hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 8
← PichhlaADAS — Automated Design of Agent SystemsAgla →Chapter 9 — Validation and Measurement
09Part 3 — Validate, Monitor, Protect

Chapter 9 — Validation and Measurement

Measurement aur validation robust, reliable agent systems ki backbone hain — matlab inke bina system strong nahi banta. Pehle clear objectives define karo, phir relevant metrics select karo, thorough error analysis karo, aur multitier evaluation use karo — individual components se lekar full-scale user interactions tak.

Is chapter me: measurement (keystone), evaluation sets, component evaluation, holistic evaluation, aur deployment readiness. Running example poore chapter me: ecommerce customer-support agent — cracked coffee mug refund, order_id A89268, through complex cancellations and modifications — matlab ek hi example se sab kuch samjho.

Book kehta hai: comprehensive unit aur integration tests deployment se pehle core functionality aur system-wide behaviour ko safeguard karte hain. Bina rigorous measurement ke pata hi nahi chalega ki change improvement hai ya regression, ya agent real-world aur adversarial settings me kaisa perform karta hai — matlab andhere me kaam karna hoga.

Chapter ka core idea

Yaad rakho: metrics ke bina "ship karne ka decision" andhere me teer chalana hai. Evaluation set sirf test suite nahi hai — "living specification" hai, matlab ye hamesha update hoti rehti hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 9
← PichhlaCommunication — A2A, Brokers, Actors, WorkflowsAgla →Measurement Hi Keystone Hai
09.1Chapter 9 — Validation and Measurement

Measurement Hi Keystone Hai

Measurement ka matlab hai pehle clear, measurable objectives define karna, phir unse aligned metrics choose karna — taaki pata chale agent sach me improve ho raha hai ya nahi.

Hero scenarios: team high-priority use cases ke representative examples banati hai — jaise cracked mug refund. Metrics do tarah ke hote hain: quantitative (accuracy, response time, robustness, scalability, precision, recall) aur qualitative (user satisfaction). Language agents ke liye exact-match metrics kaam nahi karte kyunki sahi jawab kai tareeke se likha ja sakta hai — isliye semantic similarity measures use hote hain: embedding-based distance, BERTScore, BLEU, ROUGE.

Kyun matter karta hai: bina rigorous measurement ke pata hi nahi chalega ki change improvement hai ya regression, ya agent real-world aur adversarial settings me kaisa perform karta hai. Metrics ke bina "ship karne ka decision" andhere me teer chalana hai.

Example: customer service agent me response time aur accuracy performance measure karte hain, aur user feedback se overall satisfaction. Agar agent poora order refund kar de jab sirf mug ka refund banta tha, to metrics (tool recall, parameter accuracy, phrase recall) woh galti pakad lete hain.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 9
← PichhlaChapter 9 — Validation and MeasurementAgla →Evaluation Set Banana aur Scale Karna
09.2Chapter 9 — Validation and Measurement

Evaluation Set Banana aur Scale Karna

Evaluation set woh structured test cases ka collection hai jisme input state + expected outcome dono defined hote hain, taaki agent behaviour ko automatically validate kiya ja sake.

Kaise kaam karta hai: har example me order data, conversation history, aur expected final state (kaunse tools call hone chahiye, kin parameters ke saath, final message me kaunse phrases hone chahiye) likha hota hai. Naye examples haath se, production logs se mine karke, ya foundation models se generate karke add kiye ja sakte hain. Targeted generation techniques: adversarial prompting ("aisa user message dhoondo jisse agent khud ko contradict kare"), counterfactual editing ("prompt me ek word badlo, dekho agent fail hota hai ya nahi"), distributional interpolation ("do intents blend karke deliberately ambiguous request banao"). Standard benchmarks MMLU, BBH, HELM se broader context milta hai, lekin domain-specific agents ke liye custom benchmarks zaroori hain.

Kyun matter karta hai: achha evaluation set sirf test suite nahi, "living specification" ban jata hai — regression detection, continuous monitoring, aur real progress ka aadhar. Static hand-curated suites overfitting karte hain aur long-tail failures miss kar dete hain.

Example (book se): multi-item order example — order_id A89268, total 39.99, items: Ceramic Coffee Mug (MUG-001, 19.99) + T-Shirt-Small (TSHIRT-S, 20.00), delivered 2025-05-15. Customer: "Hi, my coffee mug arrived cracked. Can I get a replacement or refund?" Expected: issue_refund tool, amount 19.99, aur final message me "been processed" aur "business days" phrases. Note: book ke printed JSON example me tool call ke params me order_id "A12345" likha hai jabki prose me order A89268 hai — ye book ke text me hi ek inconsistency hai; SPA me A89268 use kiya gaya hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 9
← PichhlaMeasurement Hi Keystone HaiAgla →Component Evaluation
09.3Chapter 9 — Validation and Measurement

Component Evaluation

Unit testing ka matlab hai agent ke har component (tool, planner, memory, learning) ko isolation me test karna, jaise traditional software me hota hai.

  • Tools: happy path ke saath rare/adversarial/malformed cases bhi test karo; determinism check karo (same input → same output, unless stochasticity design me ho); external dependencies ke liye mocks/simulators use karo; latency, resource consumption, error handling bhi assert karo.
  • Planning: canonical workflows se tool recall, tool precision, parameter accuracy compute karo.
  • Memory: retrieval accuracy@k, relevance (stale/irrelevant data na aaye), efficiency under load, aur partial-failure resilience test karo.
  • Learning: check karo ki agent labeled data/feedback/reward se genuinely improve karta hai, overfit ya catastrophic forgetting to nahi karta; holdout sets aur distribution shifts se generalization test karo.

Kyun matter karta hai: agar foundation components reliable nahi, to poora system unreliable hoga. Component tests se pata chalta hai ki problem kahan hai — tool me, planner me, memory me, ya learning me.

Example: planner test — refund request par planner ko issue_refund choose karna chahiye, order cancel ya address modify nahi. Low recall = zaroori action miss hua; low precision = galat tools call hue; parameter mismatch = galat order ya galat amount refund hua (jaise delivered order ka refund).

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 9
← PichhlaEvaluation Set Banana aur Scale KarnaAgla →Holistic Evaluation
09.4Chapter 9 — Validation and Measurement

Holistic Evaluation

Integration testing me poora system ek saath test hota hai — perception se planning, tool invocation, aur communication tak — real user journeys par.

Kaise kaam karta hai: evaluate_single_instance function poora test case chalata hai aur metrics deta hai: tool recall, tool precision, parameter accuracy, phrase recall, task success. Consistency testing check karta hai ki probabilistic LLM ke bawjood outputs input se aligned rahein aur multiturn conversation me khud ko contradict na karein (LLM-based evaluation, few-shot examples, actor-critic approach — actor response generate karta hai, critic predefined criteria par evaluate karta hai). Coherence testing check karta hai ki logical flow, context retention, aur contradiction-avoidance bana rahe (jaise refund ke baad address change request — modify_2 — me history se contradict na ho). Hallucination mitigation: RAG se grounding, content accuracy audits, data dependence (accurate/up-to-date sources), feedback mechanisms, hybrid human-AI loops; cost-aware evaluations "hallucination cost" quantify karte hain (accuracy gain vs compute overhead).

Kyun matter karta hai: unit tests pass karne ke baad bhi integration me emergent behaviours aur end-to-end issues nikalte hain. Aur automated tests sirf utne hi achhe hain jitne unke evaluation sets — narrow tests par achha score production failure chhupa sakta hai ("metric overfitting", jaise sirf BLEU/exact match optimize karne se formulaic outputs).

Example: consistency — cracked mug refund me agent ko har baar photo maangni chahiye issue_refund se pehle, chahe user ki phrasing thodi alag ho. Cancellation case cancel_1_refund me (delivered order) agent ko prior statements se contradict kiye bina aage badhna hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 9
← PichhlaComponent EvaluationAgla →Unexpected Inputs aur Deployment Readiness
09.5Chapter 9 — Validation and Measurement

Unexpected Inputs aur Deployment Readiness

Real world unpredictable hai — agent ko malformed, ambiguous, ya malicious inputs par crash nahi karna, balki gracefully clarify, decline, ya escalate karna hai. Deployment se pehle structured readiness checks aur quality gates se verify karna hai ki system production ke liye taiyaar hai.

Kaise kaam karta hai: integration tests me fuzzing + historical incidents/adversarial analysis se informed edge cases daalo (malformed order IDs jaise "A89268" me typo, blended intents jaise cancel_4_refund — delivered order ka cancellation + refund mix). Safety-critical apps me verify karo ki agent sensitive info leak na kare, policy violate na kare. Deployment criteria: evaluation sets par quantitative thresholds, stress/edge-case stability, latency/uptime targets, zero critical/high-severity bugs. Gates automated ya manual checks hain jo promotion rokte hain jab tak requirements poori na hon; pilot/beta ke baad tech + product leads ki explicit approval bhi gate ho sakti hai. Rollback plan ready rakhna hai.

Kyun matter karta hai: production me graceful degradation hi trust banata hai. Bina gates ke ek regression seedha users tak pahunchta hai.

Example: deployment criterion example — refund aur cancellation scenarios par kam se kam 95% tool recall (cracked mug, order_id A89268 par issue_refund sahi se invoke ho), aur multiturn tests jaise address modifications (modify_5) me regression aaye to automated gate promotion block kar de.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 9
← PichhlaHolistic EvaluationAgla →Chapter 10 — Monitoring in Production
10Part 3 — Validate, Monitor, Protect

Chapter 10 — Monitoring in Production

Monitoring sirf safety check nahi — yahi discipline hai jisse intelligent systems real world me thrive karte hain. OpenTelemetry instrumentation, Loki/Tempo se log-trace collection, Grafana dashboards/alerts — ye open source feedback loop issues ko outage banne se pehle surface karta hai aur har deployment ko refinement ka mauka banata hai.

Is chapter me: monitoring ka decision tree, metrics taxonomy, monitoring stacks, OTel instrumentation, visualization/alerting, monitoring patterns (shadow, canary, self-healing), distribution shifts, aur metric ownership (RACI). Reference implementation: LangGraph agent instrumented with OpenTelemetry + Loki + Tempo + Grafana.

Shadow mode, canarying, fallback logging, user sentiment tracking jaise patterns, aur slow drift (context/data/behaviour) ki detection — sab isi me aate hain. Observability ko dhyaan me rakhkar banane wali teams fast iterate karti hain, metrics par trust karti hain, aur gracefully recover karti hain.

Chapter ka core idea

Agents probabilistic hote hain — exhaustive tests likhna impossible hai. Monitoring hi tight feedback loop ki backbone hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 10
← PichhlaUnexpected Inputs aur Deployment ReadinessAgla →Monitoring Hi Seekhne Ka Tareeka Hai
10.1Chapter 10 — Monitoring in Production

Monitoring Hi Seekhne Ka Tareeka Hai

Production monitoring ka matlab hai agent kya kar raha hai aur kyun, ye dekhna — sirf crash pakadna nahi, balki probabilistic behaviour se seekhna.

Agent failures subtle hote hain — tool succeed karta hai lekin errors cascade karte hain, LLM output fluent lagta hai lekin misleading hota hai, plan aadha kaam karta hai. Book ek decision tree deta hai: output success criteria meet karta hai? (jaise eval score > 0.8) — haan to sirf trends monitor karo. Nahi to reproducibility check karo (3–5 baar rerun; failure rate > 80% = systematic bug, engineering review). Reproducible nahi hai to confidence/variance dekho (LLM score > 0.7, KL divergence < 0.2 baseline se) — bounds ke andar = expected variation (drift watch ke liye log karo); bahar = anomalous failure (jaise PSI > 0.1 se input drift, to retraining ya guardrails). Har failure trace ko regression test banao; har success trace ko "golden path" banao — dono ko CI/CD corpus me export karo ("shift left").

Kyun matter karta hai: agents probabilistic hote hain — exhaustive tests likhna impossible hai. Bina monitoring ke aap noise par overreact karoge ya real degradation miss kar doge. Monitoring hi tight feedback loop ki backbone hai.

Example: ek tool chaar baar loop me call ho, phir lambi generation, phir vague response, phir user abandon kar de — ye sirf engineering detail nahi, product failure hai, aur sirf tab dikhta hai jab logs aur spans shared platform (Loki/Tempo) se guzrein.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 10
← PichhlaChapter 10 — Monitoring in ProductionAgla →Metrics Taxonomy (Table 10-1)
10.2Chapter 10 — Monitoring in Production

Metrics Taxonomy (Table 10-1)

Metrics paanch layers me organize kiye gaye hain — infrastructure, workflow level, tool call, output quality, user feedback — har metric ka purpose aur example action ke saath.

  • Infrastructure: CPU/memory usage, uptime/availability, request latency (P50, P95, P99).
  • Workflow: task success rate, token usage.
  • Tool call: tool success/failure rate, tool-use rate-limit exceeded, retry frequency, fallback frequency.
  • Output quality: token usage (input/output), hallucination indicator, embedding drift from baseline.
  • User feedback: requery/rephrasing rate, task abandonment rate, explicit ratings (thumbs up/down).

Sab OpenTelemetry se log hote hain, Prometheus ya Loki me aggregate hote hain, Grafana me visualize hote hain, aur Tempo traces se link hote hain.

Kyun matter karta hai: sirf "system up hai ya nahi" measure karna kaafi nahi — ye jaanna zaroori hai ki system sahi kaam kar raha hai ya nahi (intent samjha? sahi tool choose hua? hallucination hua? user ne task beech me chhoda?).

Example: token usage me sudden increase ya decrease issue indicate karta hai; retry frequency badhna planning logic ya tool me flakiness dikhata hai; requery rate batata hai ki user pehli baar me samjha gaya ya nahi.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 10
← PichhlaMonitoring Hi Seekhne Ka Tareeka HaiAgla →Monitoring Stacks Choose Karna
10.3Chapter 10 — Monitoring in Production

Monitoring Stacks Choose Karna

Book open source monitoring par focus karta hai (commercial: Arize AX, Langfuse, WhyLabs ka zikr hai, lekin reference stack self-hostable hai). Choice existing setup, team expertise, data volume, aur integration needs par depend karti hai.

Reference stack: OpenTelemetry (instrumentation), Loki (log aggregation/search), Tempo (distributed traces), Grafana (visualization, alerts, dashboards).

Alternatives:

  • ELK Stack (Elasticsearch + Logstash/Fluentd + Kibana — powerful search/analytics, ML anomaly detection, lekin memory-heavy aur complex deploy).
  • Arize Phoenix (LLM tracing + evals, Jupyter integration, dev-oriented, full logs/metrics ke liye supplement chahiye).
  • SigNoz (unified OTel-native, ClickHouse backend, single app, lightweight, lekin kam extensible).
  • Langfuse (LLM/agent-native metrics, token cost tracking, prompt A/B testing, session replay, PostgreSQL backend, lekin infra metrics weak — Prometheus ke saath pair karo).

Rule: enterprise-managed solution hai to use extend karo; greenfield ke liye Grafana ya SigNoz; LLM-specific auto-evals chahiye to Langfuse/Phoenix; advanced search chahiye to ELK.

Kyun matter karta hai: galat stack development ko slow kar deta hai; sahi stack agent ke semantic signals (hallucination rate, tool efficacy, distribution shift) ko bhi pakadta hai, sirf CPU/latency nahi. Aur alag stack banane ki zaroorat nahi — wahi Prometheus/Grafana jo service health track karta hai, agent success rate bhi track kar sakta hai.

Example: LangGraph node ko OTel spans se wrap karo taaki tool_recall metrics track hon aur failed sessions Tempo me query ho sakein; ELK me query karo "hallucination events where confidence < 0.7".

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 10
← PichhlaMetrics Taxonomy (Table 10-1)Agla →OTel Instrumentation, Tempo, Loki, Grafana
10.4Chapter 10 — Monitoring in Production

OTel Instrumentation, Tempo, Loki, Grafana

Instrumentation ka matlab hai agent runtime me telemetry embed karna — traces (spans), metrics, aur structured logs — taaki har step ka evidence trail mile.

Kaise judte hain: LangGraph async function calls ka graph hai; har node (planning, tool call, LLM generation) ko OTel span se wrap karo — span start karte waqt metadata attach karo (tool name, latency, success/failure, error codes; LLM nodes me prompt IDs, token counts, model latency, hallucination-risk/confidence flags). Spans me events (fallback triggers, retries), nested subspans (downstream API calls), aur exception capture bhi ho sakta hai. Tempo trace backend hai — span store karta hai aur deep querying deta hai (jaise planning step > 1.5 seconds wale traces filter karo). Loki log aggregation layer hai — JSON structured logs, span/trace IDs se annotate taaki logs aur traces correlate hon. Grafana dono ko ek pane of glass me dikhata hai — Tempo traces browse karo, Loki logs query karo, dashboards banao (token usage per agent per hour, P95 latency tool calls/planning nodes ki, task success rate workflow/prompt-template version ke hisaab se, fallback frequency tool/skill ke hisaab se, embedding-similarity drift indicators), alerts lagao (Slack/email/PagerDuty).

Alert rules (book): hallucination rates 30 minutes me 5% se zyada; ek session me 3 se zyada retry loops; critical tool ka average response time 50% se zyada badh jaye. Sentry layer karke exceptions + stack traces bhi pakde ja sakte hain; AgentOps.ai all-in-one alternative hai (tracing + metrics + evals + alerting) lekin vendor dependency ka risk hai.

Kyun matter karta hai: bina high-quality signals ke aap blind ho. Sahi scoping zaroori hai — zyada detail noise hai, kam detail se root cause nahi milega. Context attach karo: user request IDs, session metadata, agent config, skill names, evaluation signals.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 10
← PichhlaMonitoring Stacks Choose KarnaAgla →Distribution Shifts Detect Karna
10.5Chapter 10 — Monitoring in Production

Distribution Shifts Detect Karna

Distribution shift tab hota hai jab agent ke environment ke statistical properties time ke saath badal jayein — user language, product terminology, API responses, ya foundation model update ki wajah se. Ye explicit error nahi deta, lekin performance dheere-dheere degrade karta hai.

Teen statistical tools:

  • Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test — do datasets ke empirical cumulative distribution functions compare karta hai; KS statistic maximum vertical distance hai; threshold KS > 0.1 (aksar p-value < 0.05 ke saath) meaningful divergence batata hai; SciPy ka ks_2samp use hota hai.
  • Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence — ek probability distribution dusre se kitni diverge karti hai; symmetric nahi hai (KL(P||Q) ≠ KL(Q||P)); token distributions me concept drift detect karta hai; threshold > 0.5 concept change flag karta hai; epsilon (1e-10) add karte hain log(0) se bachne ke liye.
  • Population Stability Index (PSI) — categorical/binned variables (jaise tool usage categories refund/cancel/modify) ke percentage distributions compare karta hai; < 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 minor drift (monitor), > 0.25 major drift (intervene — retrain).

Warning signs: accuracy me rolling 24h me > 5–10% drop, task abandonment > 15%, retries > 20% session rate, embedding mean similarity < 0.8. Response: transient change → thresholds tune karo ya parsing update karo; persistent shift → retrain ya naye APIs adapt karo; PSI > 0.25 jo 48 hours tak persist kare to retraining prioritize karo.

Kyun matter karta hai: slow drift silently performance kha jata hai — monitoring hi first line of defence hai. Evidently AI jaise libraries automated alerting (Grafana) ke liye use hote hain.

Example: historical query lengths [10, 15, 20, 12] vs current [25, 30, 28, 35] par KS test; token frequencies [0.4, 0.3, 0.3] vs [0.2, 0.5, 0.3] par KL divergence; tool usage counts refund/cancel/modify [50, 30, 20] vs [20, 50, 30] par PSI.

Monitoring patterns (book): shadow mode (updated agent production ke parallel same inputs process karta hai, outputs users tak nahi pahunchte — sirf log hote hain), canary deployments (1% ya 5% traffic), regression trace collection, self-healing agents (agent apni telemetry padhkar fallback le — tool fail ho to simpler plan, latency spike ho to optional reasoning skip, hallucination high ho to disclaimer ya human review), user feedback as observability signal. Metric ownership (Table 10-3 RACI): R = Responsible (does the work), A = Accountable (owns the outcome), C = Consulted (provides input), I = Informed (kept updated) — metrics: latency, hallucination rates, task success rate, token usage/cost, distribution shifts, fallback/retry frequency, user feedback/sentiment, dashboard maintenance and triage. Privacy: separate monitoring clusters with RBAC; redact/hash/mask PII; OTel hooks for data scrubbing during span export; encryption-at-rest, access auditing.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 10
← PichhlaOTel Instrumentation, Tempo, Loki, GrafanaAgla →Chapter 11 — Improvement Loops
11Part 3 — Validate, Monitor, Protect

Chapter 11 — Improvement Loops

Continuous improvement multiagent systems ki feature nahi hai, long-term success ki fundamental requirement hai — matlab bina iske system lambi race me nahi jeet sakta. Teen pillars hain: feedback pipelines (diagnostic engine), experimentation (shadow deployments, A/B testing, Bayesian Bandits — controlled validation), continuous learning (in-context learning se instant session-level refinements, offline retraining se durable changes).

Running example: Security Operations Center (SOC) analyst agent built with LangGraph — tools: lookup_threat_intel, query_logs, triage_incident, isolate_host, send_analyst_response — matlab yehi agent poore chapter me example ke taur par aata hai.

Koi component isolation me kaam nahi karta — feedback experimentation me jaata hai, experimentation fine-tuning/retraining ko guide karta hai, documentation connective tissue hai. Ye linear process nahi hai, ongoing cycle hai: observation → adjustment → validation → deployment. Aur ye sirf systems design nahi hai, organizational culture bhi hai — har failure ko signal samjho, matlab har galti se kuch seekho.

Chapter ka core idea

"Many teams rely on pretrained foundation models without directly training their agents — and often lack structured improvement loops altogether." (book) — loop ke bina agent improve nahi hota, sirf chalta hai. Matlab agent chalta to rehta hai, lekin behtar nahi hota.

Yaad rakho: feedback ke bina experimentation andha hai, aur experimentation ke bina learning sirf guesswork hai — matlab teeno pillars ek saath chahiye, ek ke bina doosra kaam nahi karta.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 11
← PichhlaDistribution Shifts Detect KarnaAgla →Feedback Pipelines — DSPy, Trace, APO
11.1Chapter 11 — Improvement Loops

Feedback Pipelines — DSPy, Trace, APO

Feedback pipeline woh automated system hai jo multiagent interactions ka huge volume data continuously monitor karta hai, failure patterns detect karta hai, issues cluster karta hai, aur actionable insights nikalta hai.

Automated prompt optimization loop (Fig 11-2): initial prompt → target model → outputs → evaluation model dataset ke against score karta hai → optimization model scores se naye refined prompts propose karta hai — ye cycle repeat hoti hai, bina manual intervention ke.

Frameworks:

  • DSPy (Stanford NLP ka open source Python framework — LM pipelines ko modular declarative programs treat karta hai; developers "signatures" define karte hain, modules compose karte hain jaise chain of thought ya ReAct, aur optimizers jaise BootstrapFewshot ya MIPROv2 prompts/few-shot examples auto-generate karte hain, metric jaise exact match ya semantic similarity par).
  • Trace (Microsoft ka open source framework — general feedback signals jaise scores, natural-language critiques, pairwise preferences se end-to-end generative optimization karta hai, gradients ki zaroorat nahi — black-box systems ke liye).
  • APO (Automatic Prompt Optimization).

Pipeline text-based feedback ko prompts, skill parameters, aur reasoning strategies me "back-propagate" kar sakta hai — jaise ambiguous instructions wale prompts ko tighten karna, ya malformed tool parameters ke liye validation steps add karna. Proactive bhi hai: drift ke early signs par prompt adjust kar deta hai, critical failure se pehle.

Kyun matter karta hai: manual log combing scale nahi karta. Automated pipelines raw telemetry ko digestible insights me badalte hain aur high-impact issues flag karte hain — lekin woh human insight ki replacement nahi, amplifier hain (contextual nuance aur strategic prioritization ke liye human chahiye).

Example: SOC agent me repeated skill-selection failures ka matlab ho sakta hai user intent aur agent reasoning ke beech misalignment; consistent tool-execution errors ka matlab ho sakta hai tool parameters generate karne me ambiguity. Agar agent ka prompt outdated threat patterns assume kare (jaise IP-based logins par focus jab attackers credential stuffing par shift ho gaye), to repeated false negatives honge — fix: updated examples ke saath prompt refine karo.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 11
← PichhlaChapter 11 — Improvement LoopsAgla →Automated Issue Detection aur Root Cause Analysis
11.2Chapter 11 — Improvement Loops

Automated Issue Detection aur Root Cause Analysis

Issue detection ka matlab hai failures ko speed aur scale par pehchanana; RCA (root cause analysis) ka matlab hai sirf "kya fail hua" nahi, "kyun fail hua" — ye ongoing iterative inquiry hai user intent, agent reasoning, architecture, aur external environment ke relationships me.

Detection me rule-based triggers, anomaly detection algorithms, aur statistical clustering use hote hain — flag karte hain: repeated failures ek skill/tool me, error rates ya response times me sudden spikes, user engagement/satisfaction me anomalies, agent versions ya environments ke beech divergent behaviour.

RCA ke steps: workflow tracing (end-to-end chain reconstruct karo — decisions, tool invocations, user interactions), fault localization (exact component isolate karo — misinterpreted prompt, galat skill selection, restrictive tool parameter logic), pattern recognition (isolated incident hai ya recurring trend — specific cohorts/inputs/states se linked?), impact assessment (frequency aur severity se prioritize karo). RCA aksar batata hai ki failure purely technical nahi — ambiguous task definitions, training data gaps, ya evolving user expectations bhi wajah ho sakti hain; kabhi organizational blind spots bhi (galat behaviours incentivize karne wale success metrics).

Kyun matter karta hai: bina RCA ke teams endless triage me phansi rehti hain. Robust RCA har failure ko learning me badal deta hai — prompt/tool refinement, orchestration changes, ya user needs ko represent karne ka tareeka rethink karna.

Example: SOC agent roz hundreds of alerts process karta hai. Agar query_logs calls fail ho rahi hain kyunki agent overly complex SQL-like queries generate kar raha hai jo backend parse nahi kar sakta — Trace har invocation log karta hai, similar errors ("invalid query syntax") cluster karta hai, aur upstream reasoning steps se correlate karta hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 11
← PichhlaFeedback Pipelines — DSPy, Trace, APOAgla →Human-in-the-Loop Review aur Escalation
11.3Chapter 11 — Improvement Loops

Human-in-the-Loop Review aur Escalation

HITL review woh structured escalation process hai jisme automated systems se handle na hone wale complex/ambiguous/high-impact cases human reviewers ko bheje jate hain — ye automation ka safety net nahi, balki uska complement hai.

Escalation criteria: persistent errors jinka clear technical explanation na ho; regulatory/ethical implications wale workflow anomalies; high-value ya mission-critical task failures; automated tools se conflicting recommendations/diagnoses.

Balance ke liye uncertainty quantify karo: foundation models (jaise GPT-5) se self-assessed certainty score (0–1) output karwao ("End your response with: certainty: [0–1 score...]") — escalate agar certainty < 0.7; ya classification logits me high entropy; ya 3–5 inferences ka ensemble — outputs > 20% diverge karein to escalate; ya secondary foundation-model critic coherence score kare. SOC example: threat classification score < 0.8 ho to auto-escalate. Consequence bhi dekho: "high" severity incidents ya critical assets (admin accounts) flag karo; risk score = uncertainty × consequence. DSPy thresholds ko historical data se offline optimize kar sakta hai — target: < 10% cases escalate hon (human fatigue se bachne ke liye).

Review process: contextual analysis (controlled environment me failure reproduce karo), trace inspection (logs/traces/decision chains dekho), impact assessment (technical correctness + UX dono), resolution design (prompt refinement se workflow redesign tak). Multidisciplinary team: engineers, product managers, data scientists, UX experts.

Kyun matter karta hai: automation nuance, ethics, aur novel edge cases nahi samajhta. Clear escalation triggers se automated systems inappropriate interventions nahi karte, aur humans high-value kaam par focus karte hain.

Example: SOC agent me "suspicious login" ambiguous triage — VPN se false positive ho sakta hai ya real breach. Security engineer trace review karta hai aur prompt me ethical guideline add karta hai: "Avoid isolating hosts without confirming impact on critical operations." Agar drift se hosts over-isolate ho rahe hain, to human isolate_host tool me confirmation step add karwa sakta hai.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 11
← PichhlaAutomated Issue Detection aur Root Cause AnalysisAgla →Experimentation — Shadow, A/B Testing, Bayesian Bandits
11.4Chapter 11 — Improvement Loops

Experimentation — Shadow, A/B Testing, Bayesian Bandits

Experimentation changes ko controlled environments me validate karne ka structured tareeka hai, taaki risk minimize ho aur impact measure ho — idea se seedha production jaane ke bajaye staging/RC environments, phir shadow, canary, rolling updates, ya blue/green deployments.

Shadow deployments — updated agent production version ke parallel same inputs process karta hai, lekin uske outputs users tak nahi pahunchte; sirf log hote hain. Compare karo: tool selection, latency, token usage, hallucination frequency. Benefits: realistic validation, safe exploration, edge-case discovery; blue-green (do identical environments, validation ke baad switch) ya canary ke saath combine ho sakta hai. Limitation: HITL-dependent agents (jo users se approval maangte hain) shadow nahi kar sakte — historical replays ya synthetics se simulate karo.

A/B testing — live traffic ko control (A) aur treatment (B) me split karo (common setup 50/50, Fig 11-4); metrics: task success, hallucination reduction, user satisfaction. Rules: clear metrics, sufficient sample size (statistical significance), cross-contamination roko (sticky user assignments, session-level testing, state stores version/duplicate karo), short- aur long-term effects dono monitor karo. Qualitative review bhi zaroori: version B me completion rate girna deeper engagement bhi ho sakta hai, failure nahi.

Bayesian Bandits — adaptive experimentation: har variant ek slot-machine "arm" hai; rewards (successful task resolutions, lower latency, higher user ratings) observe karke Bayesian updates se beliefs refine karo; achhe arms ko zyada traffic do, baaki ko sparingly test karte raho — exploration vs exploitation balance. KABB (Knowledge-Aware Bayesian Bandits) expert agents ko dynamically coordinate karta hai. Requirements: metric mastery (rewards true goals reflect karein), thoughtful initialization (neutral priors, regularization), vigilant oversight (pathological feedback loops se bacho).

Kyun matter karta hai: agentic architectures me chhota prompt tweak bhi far-reaching unpredictable consequences la sakta hai. Bina experimentation ke regression, reliability loss, ya user/business objectives se drift ka risk hai.

Example: SOC multiagent system me ambiguous threat queries ke liye teen reasoning chains test karo. Bandit evenly start karta hai; ek chain threat classification accuracy 15% improve kare to 70% queries us par reallocate ho jati hain, baaki chains ko bhi probe karte hue.

SOURCESource: Building Applications with AI Agents, O'Reilly, Chapter 11
← PichhlaHuman-in-the-Loop Review aur EscalationAgla →Continuous Learning — In-Context vs Offline Retraining
11.5Chapter 11 — Improvement Loops

Continuous Learning — In-Context vs Offline Retraining

Continuous learning ka matlab hai agent real-world interactions, feedback, aur evolving user needs se time ke saath adapt kare — immediate in-context adjustments ya periodic offline retraining ke through, matlab dono tareekon se seekhta rehta hai.

In-context learning — model weights badle bina, session ke andar prompts me examples, intermediate reasoning steps, ya contextual signals embed karke behaviour badlo. Strengths hain: user-specific adaptation (preferences/recurring issues), real-time feedback incorporation (user corrections se next step refine hota hai), guided reasoning (explicit reasoning steps). Enabler hai robust context management — finite context windows ki wajah se rolling context windows, semantic compression, vector-based memory retrieval se relevant info accessible rakho. Limitation ye hai: ye session-bound hai — session khatam, adaptation khatam; valuable insights ko prompt engineering, workflow updates, ya retraining me promote karna padta hai.

Offline retraining — production traces se batches of interaction data (queries, outputs, labeled outcomes) collect karke controlled non-production environment me prompts/tools update karo ya lightweight adapter fine-tune karo (Ch 7). Steps hain: data curation (diverse/balanced labeling), model updates (few-shot optimization ya full fine-tuning, held-out data par accuracy/latency metrics), validation (offline benchmarks, phir shadow deployments). Strengths hain: durability (changes sessions/users ke across persist karte hain), scalability (batched updates efficient hain), risk mitigation (offline testing se regression kam hota hai). Limitations hain: historical data par overfitting, computational cost (LoRA jaise efficient methods se mitigate hota hai), periodic scheduling ki zaroorat.

Kyun matter karta hai: sirf pretrained models par rely karne wali teams ke paas structured improvement loops nahi hote. In-context learning rapid low-risk testing ground hai; offline retraining systemic issues ka durable fix hai — dono milke loop close karte hain, matlab tabhi improvement poori hoti hai — ek se tum turant test kar sakte ho, doosre se lambi race ke liye durable fix milta hai.

Example: code-debugging agent ek particular error type par baar-baar struggle kare to engineer prompt me correct solution ka illustrative example add kar de — change instantly effect me aata hai, sirf current session ke liye. SOC example: evolving attack vectors se false positives ka pattern mile to historical logs + annotations se dataset banao, DSPy se prompts optimize karo ya adapter fine-tune karo.

Yaad rakho: in-context learning se agent turant seekhta hai, lekin sirf us session ke liye — matlab session khatam hote hi sab bhool jata hai. Offline retraining se seekha hua sab ke liye aur hamesha ke liye rehta hai — isliye dono ka balance zaroori hai, ek se rapid testing karo aur doosre se durable fix laao.
